title: Headache, vomiting and a red eye — urgent recognition and next decision

blocks.text: Headache, vomiting and a red eye — urgent recognition and next decision
AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-218 | Station 2 consultation | Skills A–G (and clinical assessment/judgement as applicable) | 20 minutes | AMaC educational criteria, not official PACES marks
A 65-year-old reports severe unilateral eye pain, blurred vision and vomiting over several hours. Take a focused history, assess urgency and explain your initial plan.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text:
Hook: Suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma: red painful eye, reduced vision, hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil; migraine or uveitis can resemble some symptoms.
Trap: Headache with vomiting may be ocular rather than purely neurological.

rows: “First I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.”
ABCDE when indicated; observations and immediate safety.
“I’ll ask a few questions to narrow down the cause.”

Ask about onset, halos, previous attacks, recent pupil-dilating medicines, cataract surgery and other visual symptoms. Check visual acuity, pupil size/reactivity, corneal clarity, conjunctival injection and overall condition; avoid pressing on the painful globe.
“There is a serious possibility that we should check promptly.”
Suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma: red painful eye, reduced vision, hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil; migraine or uveitis can resemble some symptoms.
“I’ll explain what happens next and why.”

Immediate emergency ophthalmology assessment, measure intraocular pressure where competent, initiate pressure-lowering therapy under specialist/local protocol and prepare for definitive laser peripheral iridotomy when indicated.
Treats sudden visual loss and severe pain as conjunctivitis
Recognises painful red eye, headache, nausea and reduced vision as emergency
Ensures same-day emergency ophthalmology/A&E transfer without self-driving
Asks onset, vision, halos, headache, nausea, medication triggers and previous episodes
Checks other eye and alternative sight-threatening causes
Instils routine antibiotics and sends home
Assesses visual acuity, pupils and gross ocular findings without delaying referral
Checks IOP if appropriate expertise/equipment; avoids pressure on painful globe
Explains possible acute angle-closure glaucoma rather than a confirmed diagnosis
Considers uveitis, keratitis and other painful red-eye causes
Calls emergency ophthalmology and follows local urgent IOP-lowering pathway
Checks contraindications and seeks specialist-directed medication and laser planning
Minimises risk of permanent sight loss
Explains urgent treatment is needed to protect vision
Confirms safe transport, support and explicit escalation arrangements

blocks.text: Patient worries about long-term consequences and asks ‘What is this? Do I need to go to hospital?’ Answer naturally; provide the scenario details when elicited. If the candidate minimises severe symptoms, ask whether going home is safe.

Q1: Why immediate referral?
Expected answer: Acute angle closure can cause rapid irreversible sight loss.

Q2: Which symptom cluster?
Expected answer: Severe eye pain/redness, blurred vision/halos, headache and nausea or vomiting.

Q3: Which examination?
Expected answer: Visual acuity, pupil and anterior eye assessment; tonometry if skilled and available.

Q4: Do you wait for formal tonometry?
Expected answer: No, refer urgently on clinical suspicion.

Q5: Who directs pressure lowering?
Expected answer: The emergency ophthalmology service using its local pathway.

“My differential includes: Suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma: red painful eye, reduced vision, hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil; migraine or uveitis can resemble some symptoms.”

“The safe next decision is: Immediate emergency ophthalmology assessment, measure intraocular pressure where competent, initiate pressure-lowering therapy under specialist/local protocol and prepare for definitive laser peripheral iridotomy when indicated.”
Red flags: Recognises painful red eye, headache, nausea and reduced vision as emergency. Ensures same-day emergency ophthalmology/A&E transfer without self-driving.
History: Asks onset, vision, halos, headache, nausea, medication triggers and previous episodes. Checks other eye and alternative sight-threatening causes.
Assessment: Assesses visual acuity, pupils and gross ocular findings without delaying referral. Checks IOP if appropriate expertise/equipment; avoids pressure on painful globe.
Diagnosis: Explains possible acute angle-closure glaucoma rather than a confirmed diagnosis. Considers uveitis, keratitis and other painful red-eye causes.
Management: Calls emergency ophthalmology and follows local urgent IOP-lowering pathway. Checks contraindications and seeks specialist-directed medication and laser planning.
Communication: Explains urgent treatment is needed to protect vision. Confirms safe transport, support and explicit escalation arrangements.

THINK: Suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma: red painful eye, reduced vision, hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil; migraine or uveitis can resemble some symptoms. SAY: explain urgency without panic. DO: Immediate emergency ophthalmology assessment, measure intraocular pressure where competent, initiate pressure-lowering therapy under specialist/local protocol and prepare for definitive laser peripheral iridotomy when indicated. NUMBERS: 20-minute PACES encounter. TRAP: Headache with vomiting may be ocular rather than purely neurological. FINISH: Delay risks permanent vision loss. Avoid reassurance or discharge with nonspecific eye drops; alert the eye team now and discuss medication triggers.
